·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·

·

第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程

items.title: Capcom announces plans to transform its RE Engine into an 'AI-generation game engine'
items.author: Rick Lane

items.text:
Capcom has been on an historic run over the last few years, delivering hit after hit during a period when many other publishers are struggling to keep their heads above water. This year alone, Capcom has released Resident Evil: Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, all of which landed to both critical acclaim and commercial success.

So now is obviously the perfect time to wade into the not-at-all controversial topic of AI-powered game development.

Yesterday, Capcom held its own tech conference titled "Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026" during which programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a talk detailing the company's future plans for its proprietary RE: Engine—which powers all the publisher's modern games. During this talk, Ishida revealed Capcom's intentions to gradually transform RE Engine into an "AI-generation game engine."

Now, it's important to stress here that what Capcom appears to mean here is an engine for the AI generation, rather than a generative AI engine. As reported by Gamebiz (via IGN), Capcom's plans are more nuanced and detailed than slapping ChatGPT into its game development workflows.

During the talk, Ishida stated that the project is called "REX", and it involves six different programs that will integrate AI and machine-learning technology into RE Engine. Some of these are designed for enhancing program performance during development. Re:Dox, for example, is a data handling program designed to translate different types of data into a common set of rules for faster processing, while RE:UI is built to provide AI-assisted optimisation the RE: engine's development tools—sort-of like adding DLSS support for Blender.

Alongside these are tools designed to make the process of game development itself faster. There's a program called RE: Runtime, which apparently allows the engine to animate large numbers of objects and characters in groups—rather than running those real-time animations individually. Most intriguing is RE: Flows. This is apparently designed to simplify the implementation of game mechanic ideas, then convert them into a standardised programming language. This sounds vibe coding-adjacent to me, though it's hard to say for certain without seeing it in action.

According to Gamebiz, Capcom says it wants to integrate all these ideas into RE Engine for several reasons. First, modern games are so massive and technically complex that data management is a huge challenge and making changes to that data takes a long time. Second, more than 2,000 people now use RE Engine, including people from many different nationalities, so Capcom wants to create a system that is universally understandable. Third, AI technology is rapidly evolving and is essential for streamlining development—a somewhat arbitrary justification that I'm not convinced by.

Broadly though, these plans fall in line with Capcom's previously declared stance on AI, where the publisher stated it "will not implement assets generated by AI into our game content", but would use it to "enhance efficiency and boost productivity" in its development pipeline. Certainly, none of these tools appear designed to create art or character models and so forth, though it seems like some of them would require AI generated or AI assisted code to function.

It's also worth noting that Capcom's approach to development has worked pretty well for it over the last ten years, earning a reputation as one of the most reliable developers around. While I can understand the desire to make game development faster and more efficient, as the old adage goes, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".

items.title: I've been skeptical about Bandai Namco's upcoming Gundam game—but then I saw this model kit's chainsaw macuahuitl
items.author: lincoln.carpenter@futurenet.com (Lincoln Carpenter)
items.summary: Doctors have confirmed it: It's physically impossible for me to turn my nose up at a mecha action game. But despite this dire prognosis, I've been suspicious
items.text:
Doctors have confirmed it: It's physically impossible for me to turn my nose up at a mecha action game. But despite this dire prognosis, I've been suspicious of Gundam Rogue Orbit—Bandai Namco's mobile suit action game coming in spring—since it was announced back in June.

The problem is the giant monsters. I'm a Gundam traditionalist. Gundam, to me, isn't about fighting aliens—it's about traumatized child war pilots becoming so psychic that their brains explode. But this week, Bandai found a way to coax me off my high horse: With an extremely sick model kit.

【全日本ホビーショー 情報解禁＆初展示✨】HG 1/144 バウバラム 情報解禁！ガンダムゲーム最新作『GUNDAM ROGUE ORBIT』より、バウバラムがHGシリーズで登場！！ホビーサイトでの続報をお待ちください！https://t.co/XoaJUr7vZa#ガンプラ #プラモデル pic.twitter.com/Y780tB7BUEOctober 2, 2026

My time at PC Gamer has coincided with my steady descent into Gundam model kit obsession: I'm currently at the stage of manually re-scribing mold lines, so the outlook is grim. As a result, I was particularly prone to react when yesterday, as part of its reveal lineup for the 2026 All Japan Model & Hobby Show, Bandai announced the HG 1/144 Bau Bahlam—a model kit incarnation of a mobile suit we'll see in Rogue Orbit. Look at this thing:

(Image credit: Bandai)The Bau Bahlam was briefly visible in Rogue Orbit's release date trailer back in September, but these model kit renders are the first time I've properly taken in the design. Here's what jumps out at me:

It's a mono-eye suit: It's factually proven that Gundam's best guys pilot mono-eye mecha, and the Bau Bahlam feels a lot like a spiritual successor to the Gouf—the classic close-quarters mobile suit first seen piloted by Ramba Ral, also known as the realest moustachioed man in the Universal Century.

It has a CHAINSAW MACUAHUITL: If you're not familiar, the macuahuitl is a very cool, sword-like Mesoamerican weapon, consisting of a wooden body with obsidian blades embedded along its sides. The Bau Bahlam iterates on that design by swapping out one side of its giant robot-scale macuahuitl with a chainsaw, and the model kit includes a mock pull-cord so it can be posed like its revving the weapon's motor.

And, for good measure, it's got spiked knuckle plates, because apparently being punched by a giant robot doesn't hurt badly enough on its own.

It's impressively menacing, and—if the mecha customization shown in the release date trailer is any indication—we'll probably be able to use its various bits on our own robot. Hopefully that includes the macuahuitl. It'd be cruel not to.

(Image credit: Bandai Namco)I still reserve the right to be obnoxious about Rogue Orbit's departure from the traditional Gundam conceptual palette once it actually launches, but rolling out impressive mecha designs like these is an effective way of softening me up in the meantime. Surely, a game willing to give its robots giant Mesoamerican chainswords has to have its heart in the right place.

Gundam Rogue Orbit launches on Steam on March 4, 2027. The HG 1/144 Bau Bahlam kit doesn't have a release date, but it's expected to be available sometime in 2027.

items.text:
J.J. Abrams' $172 Million Sci-Fi Classic Is Officially Streaming on a New Platform

©Paramount/courtesy Everett Collection

Published Oct 4, 2026, 5:20 AM EDT

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

New York, seven years after 9/11. You'd think the city had been through enough suffering at that point, so imagine throwing a going-away party in Manhattan and discovering halfway through that the evening's entertainment has been replaced by an enormous monster tearing the city to pieces. That's how simple the conceit was for this movie that didn't even have a name for months.

That movie is Cloverfield, and J.J. Abrams' found-footage monster hit has officially found a new streaming home. The 2008 movie began streaming on Peacock in the United States on October 1, where it was joined by 10 Cloverfield Lane on the same day. For anyone planning a particularly stressful double feature, Peacock has you covered.

Directed by Matt Reeves (The Batman) and produced by Abrams (Lost), Cloverfield unfolds almost entirely through footage recovered from a handheld camera following a catastrophic attack on New York City. On the eve of his departure for Japan, Rob sees his going-away party as an opportunity to confess unresolved feelings and tie up loose ends. His agenda takes an unexpected turn when a jolt shakes the revelers.

The crowd quiets down to watch news reports of an earthquake, then rushes to the roof to assess the damage. A fireball explodes on the distant horizon. A power failure follows. Confusion gives way to panic as the partygoers stumble through the blackout and into the streets and amid the human screams and one otherworldly roar, Rob and his friends must make their way through an absolutely destroyed Big Apple.

The cast is led by Michael Stahl-David (Narcos) as Rob Hawkins, alongside Lizzy Caplan (Masters of Sex) as Marlena Diamond, Jessica Lucas (Gotham) as Lily Ford, T.J. Miller (Silicon Valley) as Hud Platt, Odette Annable (Supergirl) as Beth McIntyre, Mike Vogel (Under the Dome) as Jason Hawkins, Ben Feldman (Superstore) as Travis, and Theo Rossi (Sons of Anarchy) as Antonio.

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?

BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?

03

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.

05

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?

You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.

You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.

You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.

The Wasteland

Mad Max

Blade Runner

You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.

You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.

In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.

Arrakis

You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.

Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.

You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.

items.text:
Dan Houser helped write and produce every Grand Theft Auto as well as Red Dead Redemption 2. He was president of creative at Rockstar Games, the company he co-founded with his brother Sam Houser, at the time he left in 2020. He’s now working on new projects, including a comedic open-world game, and says he can’t watch the GTA 6 gameplay reveal because it would “distract” him creatively.

In a new podcast interview with Variety, Houser admitted that despite his connection with the Grand Theft Auto franchise and the fact that his brother is still in charge of Rockstar Games, the former GTA writer has no idea what was shown in the GTA 6 gameplay reveal that premiered in August on Netflix.

“I haven’t seen it yet,” said Houser. “I will try and avoid it because I always try and avoid stuff that’s going to distract or disrupt me creatively. And given that I spend a large amount of time trying to make open-world games, and the rest of my conscious time trying to figure out innovative ways to market them, I don’t need to see what other people are [doing]. I’m always trying to think about new ways of doing it, not sit there in some kind of comparison of what I would have done differently.”

Houser further explained that he can’t really play open-world games anymore because he ends up deconstructing how the game was made, and it distracts him too much.

“I find when I play them, I can almost deconstruct the strengths and weaknesses of the team in real time, and it’s distracting,” said Houser. “I’m always thinking, ‘Well, their animation team is weak, but I think this game design is fantastic.’ And, ‘Oh, I can imagine that meeting when they discuss this feature.’ I’m not a game designer; I’m a sort of creative director. So I’m trying to always find new things that haven’t been done before, or that I can steal from older media, quite frankly, or just inspired me, or things I always thought about.”

The former Rockstar Games head writer explained that “thankfully” he’s never needed to “be the person that understands what everyone else is doing,” so he doesn’t need to play all the new open-world games. Instead, other people at his new company, Absurd Ventures, founded in 2023, play all the new open-world games that come out for him.

“I’m trying to think about new ways of doing it,” said Houser.

“So when we worked on Red Dead Redemption, as soon as we started working, I never watched another Western. I never watched The Sopranos until after I left Rockstar. I saw one episode, because my girlfriend-now-wife and I did watch the finale in real time. I’d not seen any of it before that moment. And then I watched it all during COVID. And I’m grateful. It’s so good that it would have disrupted everything I did on GTA had I watched at the time. So I really try and avoid things that I think are going to overly influence me.”

As for what Houser is working on now, he is building out a few different multimedia franchises via Absurd Ventures. So far, the company has only released audio dramas, comic books, and novels. But it’s also developing two video games based on these media franchises.

“One is an open-world comedy which is trying to really lean into comedy and character memory, and that we’ll have more information on in the next few months,” said Houser. “And the other is a dystopian sci-fi about a video game development gone very wrong, and about a rogue AI that discovered sentience. But unfortunately, it was made by two people that didn’t like each other, so it doesn’t like itself.”

items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell

items.text:
In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right.

The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar.

In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind.

Watch on YouTube

RetroSpace takes place aboard Aurora 5, a pseudo-1970s interstellar ark that has tumbled into a black hole, and somehow come away with a mild case of temporal indecision – certain areas flip between timeframes - rather than spaghettification and incomprehensible doom. You are a janitor, woken from cryo to find a lot of stuff on fire, a lot of people dead, and a lot of other people deranged and monsterfied by gene-modding. Taking up your power wrench, you set out for the habitat hub and soon become embroiled in missions assigned by a handful of coherent survivors, including a sentient AI and a talking pig fellah.

These take you out to the far corners of the space station, which is very much the main character here. There's a "garden" sector that consists of a verdant silo with a starry dome, its spiral stairs and crawlspaces leading down to what I think is a bubbling soup of fertiliser. There's a train that circles the whole facility – not a camouflaged loading screen, as with chapter breaks in Dead Space, but an actual monorail car that travels in real time. There are a lot of audiologs, hackable terminals, and comedy public safety signs or adverts. As you might expect from the devisers of chicken detective games, RetroSpace skews toward caricature, which can get obnoxious – there's an audiolog early on that pokes fun at NPCs who leave scary audiologs. Still, it feels like the devs are fundamentally committed to making an engrossing world.

There's a persistent mystique woven around the station's janitors. Propaganda posters cast you and your lost brethren as urban legends, seldom seen by regular folk because you're always up a ladder or behind a bulkhead doing whatever it is you helmeted weirdos do with those sprays and spanners. Each sector has a locked or concealed utility closet with a portal to the Janitor's Haven - an interdimensional hideaway set up by union organisers, where you'll hang out with story-critical NPCs and do the bulk of your upgrading and customising.

If the station is a peach, I'm a little less convinced so far by the tools at your disposal. On the one hand, you've got weapons such as pistols, shotguns, and rayguns, all (eventually) upgradeable. On the other, you've got more indirect or tactical accessories such as cloaking devices, computer-hacking gizmos, and propulsive fire extinguishers. On the third hand, you've got genetic engineering or Mutamods, which range from giving yourself grasshopper thighs for higher jumping, moth ears so that you heal in light, or biceps full of rhino DNA for meatier clobbering.

The gene-modding cuts both ways: when you die, you'll be cloned for free at the nearest Bacta tank equivalent, but you'll be saddled with a random cartoon affliction for your troubles. I came away from one misadventure with a body prone to uncontrollable sneezing and swearing, which did not help with subsequent attempts at stealth. Fortunately, you can purge the debuffs by siphoning genetic material from the nearest vanilla human corpse, and Aurora 5 has no shortage of those.

Within the world, you can also do things like hold up crates to block bullets, or spray paths of water to create an electricity trap before smacking a circuit box. It's all entertaining enough, but many of the ideas are overly familiar from System Shock, Bioshock and Arkane's Prey. I'm really hoping that somewhere in RetroSpace, there lurks a tool or combination of tools that is as daft in its own way as Prey's Mimic ability. Or the slapstick bullshit you get in Skin Deep.

As it is, I'm finding that I'm too often just shooting enemies because I'm unexcited by the more devious ways of avoiding or defeating them. The enemies have their moments – lop a bugman's head off, and it might sprout legs, while the manpigs are drawn to trails of blood - but a lot of the time, they're just awareness indicators you can either avoid or gun down.

If you're comfortable with how comfortable RetroSpace can feel, as a love letter to certain famous immersive sims, you'll likely be able to forgive all this. Myself, I'd say the station ambience and secretive level design are worth the occasional sense of deja-vu. I'll keep plugging on with the game, though games journalism being what it currently is, I sadly don't have time for a full review. Find out more about RetroSpace on Steam. Let me know if you spot any really sexy airvents.

items.author: Clint Worthington

items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

Austin King is the Senior Editor of Gaming at ScreenRant and has been with the site since 2020 with a focus on RPGs and tabletop games. He previously managed content for Geek to Geek Media, and has served as a writer for sites like Nintendad, Geek Fitness, and more.
In addition to his work at ScreenRant, he also hosts the Dragon Quest FM podcast and is the author of several books, including co-writing Nimbus (a #1 bestseller in 2013). His latest is the nonfiction The Dragon Quest Book, available now.
He's written about pop culture, video games, and genre studies over the course of his career. You can find him on BlueSky, X, and at Dragonquestaustin.com

It's the Halloween season, and that means many of us are looking for spooky games to play. If you have a soft spot for the Halloween storybook charm of The Nightmare Before Christmas and the colorful, playful platforming of Super Mario Bros., then there's an upcoming game on Steam that should be just about perfect for you. It perfectly blends treak-or-treat vibes with a lightheartedness that's equally cute and spooky.

The game is called Waltz and Jam, and it's a game worth keeping an eye on. The upcoming action-adventure platformer from Flyway Games combines whimsical characters with puzzle-solving gameplay and larger-than-life enemies the two protagonists must face. Like The Nightmare Before Christmas, it's an adventure for people who love fantasy mixed with a little darkness. You can view the YouTube trailer here:

At the heart of Waltz and Jam is Waltz, a soul traveling through an afterlife inspired by a reimagining of the Seven Deadly Sins. Accompanying him is Jam, his lovable spirit dog and indispensable adventure partner. Together, they journey through seven handcrafted realms, each with its own visual identity, atmosphere, secrets, puzzles, and dangers.

That premise probably brings The Nightmare Before Christmas to mind. Like Jack Skellington exploring a different holiday world, Waltz will explore lands based on the Seven Deadly Sins. There's also Jam, a loyal dog sidekick similar to Jack's own Zero. Waltz and Jam similarly embraces the idea that scary topics don't have to be purely grim and frightening, but rather strange and even adorable.

The Steam page describes the game's realms as hand-painted storybook worlds, ranging from a chaotic restaurant to a castle filled with light and shadow. There's even a vast desert. All of these levels, of course, sound similar to what you might find in any number of Super Mario Bros. games.

Waltz and Jam Looks Like The Perfect Halloween Game

Like Super Mario Bros., the gameplay in Waltz and Jam is built around platforming, puzzles, and collectibles. You can use various abilities as you explore and face a number of boss encounters. Rather than simply moving from one combat encounter to another, players are encouraged to experiment with their surroundings and figure out how the game's various tools can open new paths.

Jam is especially important to that formula. The little dog isn't merely a companion following Waltz around. Jam can transform into useful forms, including a water ball that can bounce and splash and a trampoline that can launch Waltz into the air. Waltz also collects toys with different abilities, using them to activate mechanisms and overcome obstacles, as well as dealing with enemies.

That combination of movement and environmental interaction is where Waltz and Jam looks particularly familiar to fans of Nintendo-style platformers. The appeal isn't necessarily about copying Mario games, but about capturing the same vibe. Ultimately, Waltz and Jam has the macabre storybook atmosphere that fans of The Nightmare Before Christmas should enjoy, while its colorful exploration and platforming offer the kind of playful adventure associated with Super Mario Bros.

Dhruv is a Lead Writer in Screen Rant's New TV division. He has been consistently contributing to the website for over two years and has written thousands of articles covering streaming trends, movie/TV analysis, and pop culture breakdowns.
Before Screen Rant, he was a Senior Writer for The Cinemaholic, covering everything from anime to television, from reality TV to movies.
After high school, he was on his way to become a Civil Engineer. However, he soon realized that writing was his true calling. As a result, he took a leap and never looked back.

A sci-fi show's willingness to explore ambitious and high-concept ideas alone does not guarantee its success. However, when a sci-fi series is driven by ambition and the desire to bring something novel to the table, it often ends up etching a distinct mark in the genre while appealing to die-hard fans of the genre. One of Netflix's most ambitious sci-fi shows achieves something similar in its 16-episode runtime.

Created by Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij, Netflix's The OA unfolds through the eyes of a seemingly unreliable narrator in season 1. Like its characters, viewers are prompted to question whether they should believe the protagonist's wildly fantastical story or understand that she is merely processing her trauma. Even in these moments, though, The OA does not shy away from introducing some bizarre ideas.

Quite a few sci-fi shows dabble with ideas surrounding alternate universes and interdimensional travel. Even concepts like Near-Death Experiences and Life After Death have been quite prevalent in science fiction. The OA's portrayal of these concepts, however, completely stands out because it approaches them with incredible ambition.

Some story beats in Netflix's The OA are so imaginative that they might even sound ridiculous. But the show manages to execute them in a way that feels both realistic and relatable.

The OA Isn't Afraid Of Being Wildly Imaginative

From its opening moments, The OA does not attempt to cushion its high-concept ideas with sneaky comedy or self-mockery. It demands complete sincerity from its characters and viewers even during some of its most bizarre story developments. This sincerity perfectly aligns with its themes of liberation from fear and the courage to believe in something that is far beyond our understanding.

Even the show's primary expression of magic is portrayed as a dance form that involves five movements. As absurd as it may sound on paper, the show's execution of the same has an ethereal quality that prompts viewers to imitate the dance. This is why when Netflix canceled The OA after two seasons, some fans of the show even gathered outside Netflix's headquarters and performed the movements in rebellion.

Although The OA inclines more towards science fiction, it never truly confines itself to one fixed genre. Its sci-fi elements are often riddled with spirituality and philosophy. Meanwhile, even its story shifts between neo-noir detective thriller elements reminding one of David Lynch and twisty sci-fi similar to Netflix shows like Dark and Sense8.

Even towards the end of its second season, The OA refuses to compromise on imagination. It introduces a never-seen-before meta story where it reframes itself as a fictional story within its own universe. Considering how Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij had planned a 5-season arc for the Netflix sci-fi show, it would have taken even more ambitious leaps beyond season 2.

Like many highly acclaimed sci-fi shows on Netflix, The OA, too, was a victim of premature cancellations. After two seasons, the Netflix show had many more stories to tell and ideas to explore. Yet, it was cut short long before it could realize its full vision. Interestingly, Netflix had given the show's creators the opportunity to wrap up its story with a TV movie.

However, Zal Batmanglij and Brit Marling decided to hold on to their creative integrity instead of compressing their ambition into a movie. After all these years, The OA seems to have retained its cult following. Many fans of the show endlessly discuss its story beats and even hope for its return in the near future.

If The OA returns, it would achieve a rare fate only a few shows have in the past. However, considering how brilliantly it embraced its own stranger identity and refused to sacrifice its creative vision, its continuation could benefit the sci-fi genre as a whole.

items.author: Jacob Fox
items.summary:
Jacob Fox, hardware writer

(Image credit: Future)This week I've been: trying out the X3 Superstrike and Sensei Pro gaming mice, as well as a new Logitech
items.text:
Jacob Fox, hardware writer

(Image credit: Future)This week I've been: trying out the X3 Superstrike and Sensei Pro gaming mice, as well as a new Logitech Hall effect keyboard.

What comes to mind when I say 'big brand competitive gaming mouse'? If you're anything like me, that particular Rorschach test will make you spit out the word 'expensive.' That response isn't wrong, either: just look at the big releases we've had this year.

There was the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike: $180. The Razer Viper V4 Pro: $160. The SteelSeries Rival Pro and Sensei Pro: each $180. And there's an X3 Superstrike now, too, which is $200. These are some very expensive mice.

In previous years, I would have taken a dimmer view of this. Especially given the impressively competitive rodents you can pick up from niche Chinese brands these days. The $89 Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+, for example, is a Razer Viper V3/V4 Pro clone that performs very well and is plenty comfy.

And to be honest, even if fancy big brand mice are top-tier build quality, it's still a heck of a lot of money to ask for. The Rival Pro, Sensei Pro, and Viper V4 Pro specifically are truly fantastic on the build quality front, with the latter being practically flawless and cheaper than the rest, but they're all still very expensive.

So why isn't my view quite as dim as it could be? Because all of these releases have pushed the competitive gaming mouse scene forward in a way that probably only big brands can—both in terms of being able to absorb risk and also get new tech into as many hands as possible with big marketing campaigns.

In the case of Logitech, we have probably the most radical tech of all three: haptic-inductive (analogue) clicks. Then there's Razer, which has changed the way the sensor reports its data to save battery. And SteelSeries offers a few new things: primarily ultra-wideband (UWB) wireless connectivity and some changes to how it does polling (there are hot-swappable batteries, too, but those aren't completely new).

Logitech - analogue clicks

Analogue clicks let you adjust where the mouse button actuates, meaning you can have less time between deciding to click and actually clicking. It also lets you use rapid trigger, where you can re-click your mouse button as soon as you start to lift up on your previous click.

Razer - FrameSync

FrameSync is a technology that syncs up the mouse sensor's snapshots with when its microcontroller hands off that data to your PC. This means fewer sensor snapshots are required to maintain the same responsiveness, which ultimately saves battery.

SteelSeries - UWB and "true" 8K

Ultra-wideband (UWB) lets your mouse connect to its dongle wirelessly over different frequency bands to the usual ones, supposedly improving reliability. "True" 8K refers to how, at 8 kHz polling, the mouse doesn't batch together data but sends one packet for one receipt.

Logitech's analogue clicks

(Image credit: Logitech)Logitech's Haptic Inductive Trigger System (HITS) combines, well, haptics and induction, of course. The result is the ability to change how much you need to press down your mouse button before it actuates and registers a click, with the haptics there to ensure you get the feeling of a click wherever you set it to.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about the technology underneath the Superstrike

Logitech was the first to market with this tech. In fact, the company's head of engineering told me, "We knew we had a golden nugget in our hands... so we took all the shortcuts we could." Which probably goes some way towards explaining why an improved X3 Superstrike was released just seven months later—a fact that must surely sting some early X2 Superstrike buyers.

Since Logitech launched the X2 earlier in the year, we've seen that Keyhcron has been cooking up the "next gen mouse switch" which lets you choose between optical and magnetic within one switch, though its click feeling is static, meaning you won't be adjusting it to perfectly align with the actuation like with the Superstrike. We've also seen niche brand Finalmouse show off its TMR analogue clicks.

Razer's FrameSync

(Image credit: Razer)With the Viper V4 Pro, Razer introduced FrameSync—no, not Meta's FrameSync, something else. It essentially does for mice what VRR tech does for monitors, syncing up hardware with your system's polling. FrameSync ensures the mouse sensor's optical capture sync up with the microcontroller unit (MCU), ensuring it only captures the data when the MCU is polled by the PC and asks for it.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about how Razer's FrameSync technology works

One benefit is potentially to latency and jitter, but a good sensor doesn't really struggle with those things anyway. The actual benefit is to battery life, for one simple reason: there are fewer sensor snapshots required. That's how the Viper V4 Pro manages up to 180 hours of battery life at 1 kHz polling, despite the very performant sensor.

As far as I'm aware, Razer is the only company offering this kind of tech (Motion Sync is different). And we've seen from independent testing that FrameSync is indeed doing what it says it does.

SteelSeries' UWB and "true" 8K

(Image credit: SteelSeries)SteelSeries was the last to the 2026 'new competitive mouse tech' party, and its new technologies aren't quite as exciting as the ones mentioned previously, but are still great additions to the competitive mouse industry's toolkit. The new SteelSeries mice have hot-swappable batteries, and they're done well, but it's not the first company to have done so. It's the other technologies in there that are the newer ones.

(Image credit: Future)Read more about the collection of new technologies in the Rival Pro and Sensei Pro

SteelSeries is the first company, as far as I'm aware, to use ultra-wideband (UWB) in a mouse, apart from niche Japanese brand Elecom, which announced a similar mouse just a few weeks prior. The UWB promise is for more stable and reliable wireless connectivity. SteelSeries is also offering "true" 8K, as it claims its polling doesn't bundle up data packets but sends one packet for one receipt. Elecom makes similar claims about its mouse. SteelSeries also lets you have a lower sensor polling rate than click polling rate, but I think sensor polling is more important so I'm not too fussed about that feature.

None of these technologies on their own are quite as exciting as haptic clicks or synced sensors, but if other brands follow suit and add similar features to their mice, I certainly won't be complaining.

Big brands risk it, others follow

(Image credit: Future)After learning about all that niche brands have to offer, such as Chinese ones that make 'clones' of well-known mice, I did wonder for a while whether big brands like Razer, Logitech, and SteelSeries can continue charging so much for theirs. After all, you really can get great-performing, comfy, well-built mice for much cheaper than these big companies charge for their own options.

Perhaps these big brands started wondering the same, and rather than charging less, instead decided to use their big bucks to take the risk of investing in developing new tech. I'm sure much of this was done selfishly—to have something new and shiny to offer that other brands don't—but the positive side-effect for us consumers is that these new technologies are sure to spread out across the industry.

We should remember that with all these gaming mice, the mouse makers themselves don't make all their internal components (though Logitech does design its own sensors). Sensors, switches, and the like, are usually made in collaboration with distinct manufacturers of those parts. Which means that the new mouse tech we've seen this year isn't likely to be wrapped up with just one brand forever, unless the companies have very deep hooks in patents and whatnot.

(Image credit: Future)The fact that it's the big brands that have been taking on the risk of developing and implementing new tech also has the benefit of giving these technologies a stamp of legitimacy plus widespread marketing. Not everyone is a competitive mouse enthusiast, and most probably won't try a niche brand's mouse tech, however good it might be.

But taking the Superstrike as a paradigmatic example, Logitech is a big enough brand and has put enough marketing into its haptic-inductive click tech that people generally now accept that the technology is legitimate, useful, and marketable. Thus why other brands haven't been scared to follow suit. No doubt it helps to have some working models in the wild to see exactly how to make it work technically well, too.

All of this is to say that yes, top-tier competitive mice from big brands are ridiculously expensive these days. And yes, I'd still recommend picking up one of the many cheaper but still-quality options out there instead if you don't have a big budget. But I also have to hand it to the big brands for actually pushing the industry forwards in a way that's likely to stick. Rising tides to raise all boats, y'know?

items.text:
To most, the highlight of this week's big Deadlock patch is the snazzy map makeover, new heroes, and tons of quality-of-life additions. To me, it's all about the patch notes.

I spend a lot of waking hours reading white-text-on-black-background changelogs in this line of work, so when a page comes along that was specifically designed to be pleasant and exciting, it deserves to be rewarded. Valve has a long history of designing beautiful, bespoke webpages to introduce meaningful changes to its games, but the graphics department is really going ballistic with Deadlock.

ValveValveValveValve

(Image credit: Valve)

(Image credit: Valve)The City Never Sleeps patch notes are styled like a tourism brochure for Deadlock's refreshed New York City, walking readers through scenic stops across the four major districts (Chinatown, Theater, Haunted Lot, and Plaza). Descriptions weave between in-world storytelling and technical explanation where it makes sense, with Valve's splashes of humor reminding readers not to take any of this too seriously.

(Image credit: Valve)Dotted lines draw the reader to new points of interest as they scroll while furthering the map motif, and the page is stuffed with custom artwork for new items and mechanics that might only exist there. Valve did such an annoyingly good job with presenting the next era of Deadlock that I'm almost tempted to play a MOBA (but only almost).

Finally, some good food. Welcome back, Valve patch notes.

Valve's golden age of patch notes

September 30, 2010: The Mann-conomy Update (Image credit: Valve)It cannot be understated that Valve pioneered storytelling in multiplayer shooters with Team Fortress 2, arguably kicking off with the 2009 WAR! Update, aka "Soldier vs. Demo." This was before the concept of multiplayer games having seasons, before League of Legends had a TV show, before "live service" was even a thing—Valve had created a cast of nine lovable weirdos and new updates that weren't just dropping items, but telling stories that put the characters in conflict with one another and added context to the multiplayer maps we'd already been fighting in for two years.

It was weird in the first place for an FPS to receive so many free post-launch additions, and it was even weirder for a developer to treat the arrival of new weapons, modes, and hats as worthy of dedicated splash pages with accompanying comic books.

TF2 was the gold standard for post-launch support, and its patch notes drew massive interest, often dropping late on a Thursday or Friday, Pacific time, hinting that Valve may have been polishing until the last minute. Valve's blog posts were never the same month-to-month, often adopting new color schemes, layouts, and original elements for the occasion.

February 24, 2009: The Scout Update (Image credit: Valve)July 8, 2010: The Engineer UpdateValveJune 27, 2012: PyromaniaValveFebruary 24, 2009: The Scout UpdateValveDecember 17, 2009: WAR! UpdateValveThere was no single template they stuck to. The Engineer update introduced his advanced Gunslinger gauntlet and Wrangler as blueprints with hand-written notes, while Scout's update debuted the Force-A-Nature scattergun in a department store catalog. I especially love announcing the Mac version of TF2 with a white, sanitized home page complete with symmetrical boxes and tiny text in the style of Apple circa 2002.

June 10, 2010: The Mac Update (Image credit: Valve)Poring over the "history" section of the TF2 website in 2026 is like uncovering one of those lost civilizations that invented a ton of sophisticated things before everyone else.

April 14, 2011: The Hatless Update (Image credit: Valve)We're in an era marked by formulaic seasons, videogames as advertisement platforms, and teams scrambling to alter plans when they're not immediately popular. items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.
12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan

This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.

If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.
13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam

On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.
